claim: Cell-cell fusion is essential for tissue development.
source: Cell-cell fusion, which is essential for tissue development and used by some viruses to form pathological syncytia, is typically driven by fusogenic membrane proteins with tall (>10 nm) ectodomains that undergo conformational changes to bring apposing membranes in close contact prior to fusion.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental support in this manuscript.

claim: Some viruses use cell-cell fusion to form pathological syncytia.
source: Cell-cell fusion, which is essential for tissue development and used by some viruses to form pathological syncytia, is typically driven by fusogenic membrane proteins with tall (>10 nm) ectodomains that undergo conformational changes to bring apposing membranes in close contact prior to fusion.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Typical fusogenic membrane proteins have tall (>10 nm) ectodomains.
source: Cell-cell fusion, which is essential for tissue development and used by some viruses to form pathological syncytia, is typically driven by fusogenic membrane proteins with tall (>10 nm) ectodomains that undergo conformational changes to bring apposing membranes in close contact prior to fusion.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Fusogenic membrane proteins undergo conformational changes to bring apposing membranes in close contact prior to fusion.
source: Cell-cell fusion, which is essential for tissue development and used by some viruses to form pathological syncytia, is typically driven by fusogenic membrane proteins with tall (>10 nm) ectodomains that undergo conformational changes to bring apposing membranes in close contact prior to fusion.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The reptilian orthoreovirus p14 is a viral fusogen with a short (<2 nm) ectodomain.
source: Here we report that a viral fusogen with a short (<2 nm) ectodomain, the reptilian orthoreovirus p14, accomplishes the same task by hijacking the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work on p14 ectodomain size.

claim: Phosphorylation of the cytoplasmic domain of p14 triggers N-WASP-mediated assembly of a branched actin network.
source: We show that phosphorylation of the cytoplasmic domain of p14 triggers N-WASP-mediated assembly of a branched actin network.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Fusion is abrogated when binding of an adaptor protein to p14 is prevented.
source: Using p14 mutants, we demonstrate that fusion is abrogated when binding of an adaptor protein is prevented and that direct coupling of the fusogenic ectodomain to branched actin assembly is sufficient to drive cell-cell fusion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data with p14 mutants.

claim: Direct coupling of the fusogenic ectodomain to branched actin assembly is sufficient to drive cell-cell fusion.
source: Using p14 mutants, we demonstrate that fusion is abrogated when binding of an adaptor protein is prevented and that direct coupling of the fusogenic ectodomain to branched actin assembly is sufficient to drive cell-cell fusion.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data with engineered fusion proteins.

claim: Cell-cell fusion plays a critical role in the development of multicellular organisms, beginning with fertilization.
source: Cell-cell fusion plays a critical role in the development of multicellular organisms, beginning with fertilization and continuing with formation of muscles, osteoclasts, and the placenta in mammals.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Cell-cell fusion is involved in formation of muscles, osteoclasts, and the placenta in mammals.
source: Cell-cell fusion plays a critical role in the development of multicellular organisms, beginning with fertilization and continuing with formation of muscles, osteoclasts, and the placenta in mammals.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Some viral pathogens cause infected cells to fuse with their neighbors, creating syncytia that contribute to disease pathology.
source: Viral pathogens, including some members of poxvirus, paramyxovirus, herpesvirus, retrovirus, aquareovirus and orthoreovirus, cause infected cells to fuse with their neighbors, creating syncytia that contribute to disease pathology (Compton and Schwartz, 2017; Domachowske and Rosenberg, 1999; Moss, 2006; Smith et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The molecules and pathways responsible for cell-cell fusion are less well understood than those for enveloped virus entry and SNARE-mediated intracellular vesicle fusion.
source: While the basic steps of membrane fusion have been extensively investigated in the context of enveloped virus entry and SNARE-mediated intracellular vesicle fusion (Südhof and Rothman, 2009), the molecules and pathways responsible for cell-cell fusion are less well understood.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Syncytin-1 is involved in placental syncytiotrophoblast formation.
source: The best studied cell-cell fusogens are those with similarities to enveloped viral fusogens, including syncytin-1 (placental syncytiotrophoblasts formation) (Gong et al., 2005; Renard et al., 2005), Hap2 (conserved in eukaryotic gamete fusion) (Fédry et al., 2017; Feng et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2008b; Mori et al., 2006; Valansi et al., 2017; von Besser et al., 2006), and Eff-1/Aff-1 (C. elegans epithelial fusion) (Mohler et al., 2002; Pérez-Vargas et al., 2014; Sapir et al., 2008; Shemer et al., 2004; Zeev-Ben-Mordehai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Hap2 is conserved in eukaryotic gamete fusion.
source: The best studied cell-cell fusogens are those with similarities to enveloped viral fusogens, including syncytin-1 (placental syncytiotrophoblasts formation) (Gong et al., 2005; Renard et al., 2005), Hap2 (conserved in eukaryotic gamete fusion) (Fédry et al., 2017; Feng et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2008b; Mori et al., 2006; Valansi et al., 2017; von Besser et al., 2006), and Eff-1/Aff-1 (C. elegans epithelial fusion) (Mohler et al., 2002; Pérez-Vargas et al., 2014; Sapir et al., 2008; Shemer et al., 2004; Zeev-Ben-Mordehai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Eff-1/Aff-1 are involved in C. elegans epithelial fusion.
source: The best studied cell-cell fusogens are those with similarities to enveloped viral fusogens, including syncytin-1 (placental syncytiotrophoblasts formation) (Gong et al., 2005; Renard et al., 2005), Hap2 (conserved in eukaryotic gamete fusion) (Fédry et al., 2017; Feng et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2008b; Mori et al., 2006; Valansi et al., 2017; von Besser et al., 2006), and Eff-1/Aff-1 (C. elegans epithelial fusion) (Mohler et al., 2002; Pérez-Vargas et al., 2014; Sapir et al., 2008; Shemer et al., 2004; Zeev-Ben-Mordehai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Viral and cell-cell fusogens have tall ectodomains that typically extend more than 10 nm from the membrane in their metastable pre-fusion state.
source: A key feature of viral and cell-cell fusogens is their tall ectodomains, which in their metastable pre-fusion state typically extend more than 10 nm from the membrane.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The plasma membrane of cells is densely decorated with glycoproteins and glycolipids that could sterically block membranes from getting close enough to fuse.
source: Since the plasma membrane of cells is densely decorated with glycoproteins and glycolipids that could sterically block membranes from getting close enough to fuse, the tall ectodomains of viral and cell-cell fusogens may allow them to reach across the membrane gap and anchor to the apposing membrane, involving insertion of a fusion peptide for Class I viral fusogens or a fusion loop for Class II (Harrison, 2015; Podbilewicz, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Tall ectodomains of viral and cell-cell fusogens may allow them to reach across the membrane gap and anchor to the apposing membrane.
source: Since the plasma membrane of cells is densely decorated with glycoproteins and glycolipids that could sterically block membranes from getting close enough to fuse, the tall ectodomains of viral and cell-cell fusogens may allow them to reach across the membrane gap and anchor to the apposing membrane, involving insertion of a fusion peptide for Class I viral fusogens or a fusion loop for Class II (Harrison, 2015; Podbilewicz, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the function of tall ectodomains, supported by citations.

claim: Class I viral fusogens insert a fusion peptide into the apposing membrane.
source: Since the plasma membrane of cells is densely decorated with glycoproteins and glycolipids that could sterically block membranes from getting close enough to fuse, the tall ectodomains of viral and cell-cell fusogens may allow them to reach across the membrane gap and anchor to the apposing membrane, involving insertion of a fusion peptide for Class I viral fusogens or a fusion loop for Class II (Harrison, 2015; Podbilewicz, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Class II viral fusogens insert a fusion loop into the apposing membrane.
source: Since the plasma membrane of cells is densely decorated with glycoproteins and glycolipids that could sterically block membranes from getting close enough to fuse, the tall ectodomains of viral and cell-cell fusogens may allow them to reach across the membrane gap and anchor to the apposing membrane, involving insertion of a fusion peptide for Class I viral fusogens or a fusion loop for Class II (Harrison, 2015; Podbilewicz, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Conformational changes in fusogens cause them to fold back, pulling two membranes into close contact and forming a stable post-fusion structure that promotes membrane fusion.
source: Once the fusogen links the two membranes, conformational changes cause the fusogen to fold back, pulling the two membranes into close contact and forming a stable post-fusion structure that promotes membrane fusion (Bullough et al., 1994; Chen et al., 1999; Harrison, 2015; Ivanovic and Harrison, 2015; Pancera et al., 2014; Podbilewicz, 2014; Sapir et al., 2008; Wilson et al., 1981).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Conformational change, fusogen oligomerization, and local cooperativity are believed to provide the energy required to overcome the repulsive hydration barrier.
source: This conformational change, together with fusogen oligomerization and local cooperativity, is believed to be sufficient to provide the energy required to overcome the repulsive hydration barrier, which prevents membranes from coming closer than ~2 nm (Chernomordik and Kozlov, 2003; Harrison, 2015; Ivanovic and Harrison, 2015; Pérez-Vargas et al., 2014; Rand and Parsegian, 1989).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The repulsive hydration barrier prevents membranes from coming closer than ~2 nm.
source: This conformational change, together with fusogen oligomerization and local cooperativity, is believed to be sufficient to provide the energy required to overcome the repulsive hydration barrier, which prevents membranes from coming closer than ~2 nm (Chernomordik and Kozlov, 2003; Harrison, 2015; Ivanovic and Harrison, 2015; Pérez-Vargas et al., 2014; Rand and Parsegian, 1989).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Some transmembrane proteins required for fusion are short and do not appear to undergo conformational changes.
source: However, in other instances of cell-cell fusion, transmembrane proteins required for fusion are short by comparison and do not appear to undergo conformational changes, raising the question of how they bring two plasma membranes into close contact (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: p14 is a non-structural, single-pass transmembrane protein expressed after viral entry.
source: One example is the reptilian orthoreovirus fusion protein p14, a non-structural, single-pass transmembrane protein, that is expressed after viral entry.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: p14 is one of seven members of the FAST family of reovirus fusion proteins.
source: One of seven members of the FAST family of reovirus fusion proteins discovered by Duncan and colleagues (Ciechonska and Duncan, 2014; Corcoran and Duncan, 2004; Dawe and Duncan, 2002; Duncan et al., 1995; Duncan et al., 2004; Guo et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2015; Racine et al., 2009; Shmulevitz et al., 2004; Shmulevitz and Duncan, 2000; Wilcox and Compans, 1982), p14 has a membrane-disruptive ectodomain that is necessary to drive cell-cell fusion but extends only 0.7–1.5 nm from the plasma membrane (Corcoran et al., 2004; Corcoran et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: p14 has a membrane-disruptive ectodomain that extends only 0.7–1.5 nm from the plasma membrane.
source: One of seven members of the FAST family of reovirus fusion proteins discovered by Duncan and colleagues (Ciechonska and Duncan, 2014; Corcoran and Duncan, 2004; Dawe and Duncan, 2002; Duncan et al., 1995; Duncan et al., 2004; Guo et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2015; Racine et al., 2009; Shmulevitz et al., 2004; Shmulevitz and Duncan, 2000; Wilcox and Compans, 1982), p14 has a membrane-disruptive ectodomain that is necessary to drive cell-cell fusion but extends only 0.7–1.5 nm from the plasma membrane (Corcoran et al., 2004; Corcoran et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The p14 ectodomain has minimal secondary structure.
source: This short ectodomain has minimal secondary structure but is sufficient to disrupt opposing membranes either when added as a soluble fragment or when bare liposomes containing p14 are brought into close apposition through divalent cations (Corcoran et al., 2004; Top et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The p14 ectodomain is sufficient to disrupt opposing membranes when added as a soluble fragment.
source: This short ectodomain has minimal secondary structure but is sufficient to disrupt opposing membranes either when added as a soluble fragment or when bare liposomes containing p14 are brought into close apposition through divalent cations (Corcoran et al., 2004; Top et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Bare liposomes containing p14 can fuse when brought into close apposition through divalent cations.
source: This short ectodomain has minimal secondary structure but is sufficient to disrupt opposing membranes either when added as a soluble fragment or when bare liposomes containing p14 are brought into close apposition through divalent cations (Corcoran et al., 2004; Top et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Expression of p14 alone in cultured cells is sufficient to drive fusion with neighboring naïve cells.
source: Yet, expression of p14 alone in cultured cells is sufficient to drive fusion with neighboring naïve cells (Corcoran and Duncan, 2004; Duncan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Expression of p14 in HEK293T cells causes the cells to fuse with neighboring wild-type and p14-expressing cells, forming large multinucleated syncytia over 24 hr.
source: Expression of p14 in HEK293T cells caused the cells to fuse with neighboring wild-type and p14-expressing cells, forming large multinucleated syncytia over the course of 24 hr (Figure 1b, Video 1), like previous reports for other cell types (Corcoran and Duncan, 2004).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and Video 1.

claim: Partial cleavage of the p14 cytoplasmic tail occurs during reptilian orthoreovirus infection.
source: Partial cleavage of the p14 cytoplasmic tail, which also occurs during reptilian orthoreovirus infection (Top et al., 2009), liberates the C-terminus mCherry fluorescent tag from the transmembrane protein and serves as a convenient cytoplasmic marker of p14-expressing cells (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,b, and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and experimental data shown in figures.

claim: At 12 hr post transfection, 5% of p14-expressing cells had 3 or more nuclei.
source: At 12 hr post transfection, 5% of p14-expressing cells had 3 or more nuclei.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: At 24 hr post transfection, 34% of p14-expressing cells had 3 or more nuclei.
source: At 24 hr post transfection, 34% of p14-expressing cells had 3 or nuclei (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c and d.

claim: At 24 hr post transfection, no multinucleated cells were seen in cells transfected with mCherry alone.
source: In comparison, at 24 hr post transfection, no multinucleated cells were seen in cells transfected with mCherry alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a control experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The increase in YFP intensity in p14-expressing cells between 12 hr and 24 hr post transfection compared well with the increase in the percent of multinucleated cells.
source: Repeating the cell-cell fusion experiments above, the increase in YFP intensity in p14-expressing cells between 12 hr and 24 hr post transfection compared well with the increase in the percent of multinucleated cells, as quantified by counting nuclei (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain of p14 is comparatively long (68 amino acids).
source: While the ectodomain of p14 is shorter than typical viral fusogens, its cytoplasmic domain is comparatively long (68 amino acids).
evidence: This is stated as a factual observation about p14 structure.

claim: p14 Δcyto (Q70-I125 truncation) was properly trafficked to the plasma membrane.
source: Although p14 Δcyto was properly trafficked to the plasma membrane (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f,g and h), cell-cell fusion was abrogated (Figure 1g, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f,g,h.

claim: p14 Δcyto (Q70-I125 truncation) abrogates cell-cell fusion.
source: Although p14 Δcyto was properly trafficked to the plasma membrane (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f,g and h), cell-cell fusion was abrogated (Figure 1g, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 1i.

claim: The cytoplasmic tail of p14 is important for cell-cell fusion.
source: This is consistent with previous findings (Corcoran and Duncan, 2004), suggesting that p14 may be interacting with cellular components through its cytoplasmic tail to enable cell-cell fusion.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The p14 cytoplasmic tail is mostly disordered.
source: The p14 cytoplasmic tail is mostly disordered but has several tyrosines that could be phosphorylated (Figure 2a, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated and supported by disorder prediction shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The p14 cytoplasmic tail has several tyrosines that could be phosphorylated.
source: The p14 cytoplasmic tail is mostly disordered but has several tyrosines that could be phosphorylated (Figure 2a, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated and illustrated in Figure 2a.

claim: p14 is phosphorylated on tyrosine residues.
source: To determine if these tyrosines are indeed phosphorylated, we immunoprecipitated p14 and probed with an anti-phosphotyrosine antibody, which confirmed p14 phosphorylation (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Only the Y116F mutation decreased cell-cell fusion among the tyrosine to phenylalanine mutations tested.
source: Next, we mutated each predicted tyrosine to phenylalanine (Y59F, Y77F, Y96F, Y100F, Y116F) and found that only one mutation (Y116F) decreased cell-cell fusion (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: NetPhos3.1 and Scansite 4.0 predicted that Y116 is phosphorylated by c-src kinase.
source: We then used NetPhos3.1 and Scansite 4.0 to analyze the cytoplasmic tail of p14, and they predicted that Y116 is phosphorylated by c-src kinase (Figure 2d; Blom et al., 2004; Obenauer et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a computational prediction supported by citations to the prediction tools.

claim: Y116 phosphorylation increased when p14 YEY mutant was co-expressed with constitutively active c-src.
source: To test this prediction, we mutated all other predicted phosphotyrosines of p14 to phenylalanine (YEY; Y59F, Y77F, Y96F, Y100F) and co-expressed it with constitutively active c-src mutant (CA c-src; Y527F). Y116 phosphorylation subsequently increased, indicating c-src phosphorylates p14 (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Y116 phosphorylation increased when cells were treated with pervanadate.
source: Consistent with this, Y116 phosphorylation was also increased when tyrosine phosphatases were broadly inhibited by addition of pervanadate (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: CA c-src is sufficient to phosphorylate p14 cytoplasmic tail peptide in vitro.
source: We found that CA c-src was sufficient to phosphorylate p14 cytoplasmic tail peptide, but KD c-src was not (Figure 2f), showing that c-src kinase is sufficient to phosphorylate Y116 in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: KD c-src was not sufficient to phosphorylate p14 cytoplasmic tail peptide in vitro.
source: We found that CA c-src was sufficient to phosphorylate p14 cytoplasmic tail peptide, but KD c-src was not (Figure 2f), showing that c-src kinase is sufficient to phosphorylate Y116 in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: SYF + c-src cells fused more than SYF cells when expressing p14 WT.
source: To verify this in live-cells, we expressed p14 WT in mouse embryonic fibroblasts lacking src, yes, and fyn kinase (SYF), as well as SYF cells supplemented with c-src (SYF + c-src). Despite lower transfection efficiency and reduced cell-cell fusion compared to HEK239T cells, SYF + c-src cells fused more than SYF cells (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: c-src phosphorylates Y116 in the p14 cytoplasmic tail to drive cell-cell fusion.
source: Altogether, this demonstrates that c-src phosphorylates Y116 in the p14 cytoplasmic tail to drive cell-cell fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings.

claim: ELM predicted that phosphorylated Y116 binds to the SH2 domain of Grb2 as part of a Grb2 consensus-binding motif, YVNI.
source: ELM predicted that phosphorylated Y116 binds to the SH2 domain of Grb2 as part of a Grb2 consensus-binding motif, YVNI (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a computational prediction using the ELM tool.

claim: p14 binds to Grb2.
source: To test this prediction, we carried out a co-immunoprecipitation assay and confirmed that p14 binds to Grb2 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: p14 mutants Y116F, N118A, and FVAI severely attenuated cell-cell fusion.
source: While trafficking to the plasma membrane was intact, all three mutants severely attenuated cell-cell fusion (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b and c), suggesting that Grb2 is important for p14-mediated fusion.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c and supplementary figures.

claim: Grb2 is important for p14-mediated fusion.
source: While trafficking to the plasma membrane was intact, all three mutants severely attenuated cell-cell fusion (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b and c), suggesting that Grb2 is important for p14-mediated fusion.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data with Grb2 binding mutants.

claim: Only phosphorylated Y116 bound to Grb2 in vitro.
source: Consistent with our co-immunoprecipitation results, only phosphorylated Y116 bound to Grb2 (Figure 3d, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1e.

claim: GFP-labeled Grb2 co-localized and enriched with p14 at the plasma membrane when p14 Y116 phosphorylation is increased.
source: When p14 Y116 phosphorylation is increased in cells with either co-expression of CA c-src or addition of the phosphatase inhibitor pervanadate, GFP-labeled Grb2 co-localized and enriched with p14 at the plasma membrane (Figure 3e and f).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e and f.

claim: Grb2 did not co-localize or enrich with p14 FVAI at the plasma membrane when co-expressed with CA src or treated with pervanadate.
source: However, Grb2 did not co-localize or enrich with p14 at the plasma membrane when the Grb2 binding site was mutated to FVAI and co-expressed with CA src or treated with pervanadate (Figure 3e and f, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1f and g).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e, f and supplementary figures.

claim: The N-terminal SH3 domain of Grb2 binds to SOS, activating Ras, which in turn activates Raf kinase and the MAPK-ERK1/2 pathway.
source: The N-terminal SH3 domain of Grb2 binds to SOS, activating Ras, which in turn activates Raf kinase and the MAPK-ERK1/2 pathway, while the C-terminal SH3 domain of Grb2 binds to the actin nucleation promoting factor N-WASP, which binds to Arp2/3 and nucleates branched actin assembly (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 4a.

claim: The C-terminal SH3 domain of Grb2 binds to N-WASP, which binds to Arp2/3 and nucleates branched actin assembly.
source: The N-terminal SH3 domain of Grb2 binds to SOS, activating Ras, which in turn activates Raf kinase and the MAPK-ERK1/2 pathway, while the C-terminal SH3 domain of Grb2 binds to the actin nucleation promoting factor N-WASP, which binds to Arp2/3 and nucleates branched actin assembly (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 4a.

claim: Treatment with sorafenib tosylate, an inhibitor of Raf kinase, had no effect on cell-cell fusion at up to 100 times the IC50.
source: To determine if one or both pathways are important for fusion, we first treated cells expressing p14 with sorafenib tosylate, an inhibitor of Raf kinase, but found no effect on cell-cell fusion at up to 100 times the IC50 (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Treatment with wiskostatin, an inhibitor of N-WASP, significantly reduced cell-cell fusion.
source: We next considered whether branched actin networks could be directly involved in p14-mediated cell-cell fusion. Building on previous work showing that cytochalasin D disrupts fusion of p14-expressing cells (Salsman et al., 2008), we treated p14-expressing cells with wiskostatin, an inhibitor of N-WASP. We found that p14 trafficking to the plasma membrane fusion was unperturbed, but cell-cell fusion was significantly reduced (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b and supplementary figures.

claim: Treatment with CK-666 to inhibit the Arp2/3 complex reduced fusion in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We then treated p14-expressing cells with CK-666 to inhibit the Arp2/3 complex, which nucleates branched actin filaments, and found that fusion was reduced in a dose-dependent manner despite proper trafficking of p14 to the plasma membrane (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b and supplementary figures.

claim: Treatment with smifH2, an inhibitor of formins, enhanced cell-cell fusion.
source: Interestingly, treating p14-expressing cells with smifH2, an inhibitor of formins, enhanced cell-cell fusion (Figure 4b), perhaps due to increased branched actin assembly that has been observed when formins are broadly inhibited (Burke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Overexpression of Grb2 N-terminal mutant that can bind only to SOS reduced p14-mediated cell-cell fusion.
source: However, when the Grb2 N-terminal mutant that can bind only to SOS (Nterm) was over-expressed, the extent of p14-mediated cell-cell fusion was reduced, similar to when endogenous Grb2 binding was reduced by overexpression of the Grb2 SH2 domain (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d,e and f).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c and supplementary figures.

claim: Overexpression of Grb2 C-terminal mutant that can bind only to N-WASP restored p14-mediated cell-cell fusion to a level comparable to that of endogenous Grb2 in WT cells.
source: When a Grb2 C-terminal mutant that can bind only to N-WASP (Cterm) was over-expressed, p14-mediated cell-cell fusion was restored to a level comparable to that of endogenous Grb2 in WT cells (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d,e and f).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c and supplementary figures.

claim: The extent of p14-mediated cell-cell fusion was attenuated in N-WASP -/- cells compared to wild-type mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
source: To further confirm the specificity of N-WASP-nucleated branched actin assembly in p14-mediated cell-cell fusion, we expressed p14 WT in N-WASP null (N-WASP -/-) mouse embryonic fibroblasts. We found that the extent of p14-mediated cell-cell fusion was attenuated in N-WASP -/- cells compared to wild-type mouse embryonic fibroblasts (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1g.

claim: When Y116 of the p14 cytoplasmic tail peptide was phosphorylated, actin tails were nucleated from the bead in vitro.
source: When Y116 of the p14 cytoplasmic tail peptide was phosphorylated, actin tails were nucleated from the bead (Figure 4e), but when Y116 was not phosphorylated, actin tails were not observed (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: When Y116 of the p14 cytoplasmic tail peptide was not phosphorylated, actin tails were not observed in vitro.
source: When Y116 of the p14 cytoplasmic tail peptide was phosphorylated, actin tails were nucleated from the bead (Figure 4e), but when Y116 was not phosphorylated, actin tails were not observed (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Grb2 is necessary and sufficient to recruit N-WASP to the p14 cytoplasmic tail and can nucleate localized branched actin networks when p14 is present.
source: This confirms that Grb2 is necessary and sufficient to recruit N-WASP to the p14 cytoplasmic tail and can nucleate localized branched actin networks when p14 is present.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro actin motility assay results.

claim: Cell-cell fusion was abolished when ectodomain deletion mutant (Δecto) and cytoplasmic tail deletion mutant (Δcyto) were co-expressed in the same cell.
source: To test the necessity for direct coupling, we co-expressed the ectodomain deletion mutant (Δecto; ΔM1-T35), which traffics to the plasma membrane and binds Grb2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a and b) and the cytoplasmic tail deletion mutant (Δcyto) in the same cell. Interestingly, we found that cell-cell fusion was abolished (Figure 5a, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1c), despite the presence of both halves of p14.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a and supplementary figures.

claim: Actin assembly localized to the p14 ectodomain is necessary to drive fusion.
source: This indicates that actin assembly localized to the p14 ectodomain is necessary to drive fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-expression experiment with Δecto and Δcyto.

claim: Native Arp2/3-generated branched actin networks at cell-cell contacts are not sufficient to cause spontaneous cell-cell fusion.
source: This also suggests why native Arp2/3-generated branched actin networks at cell-cell contacts (Efimova and Svitkina, 2018) are not sufficient to cause spontaneous cell-cell fusion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental finding that direct coupling is necessary, with citation support.

claim: Expression of SH2-R47 fusion protein together with p14 in HEK293T resulted in significantly higher cell-cell fusion than when the SH2 domain lacking R47 was expressed.
source: When we expressed this fusion protein (SH2-R47) together with p14 in HEK293T, cell-cell fusion was significantly higher than when the SH2 domain lacking R47 was expressed to a similar level (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 1e,f and g).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c and supplementary figures.

claim: Direct coupling of branched actin assembly to p14 is necessary and sufficient for fusion.
source: This result demonstrates that direct coupling of branched actin assembly to p14 is necessary and sufficient for fusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SH2-R47 rescue experiment.

claim: The reptilian orthoreovirus fusogen p14 hijacks branched actin network assembly to drive cell-cell fusion.
source: This study reveals how a viral pathogen hijacks branched actin network assembly to drive cell-cell fusion, reminiscent of how the pathogens Listeria monocytogenes and vaccinia virus hijack branched actin network assembly to move within and between cells (Welch and Way, 2013).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data and citation to similar mechanisms.

claim: p14 presents a c-src kinase substrate in its cytoplasmic tail.
source: Here we show that the reptilian orthoreovirus fusogen p14 accomplishes this by presenting a c-src kinase substrate in its cytoplasmic tail, binding the host cell adaptor protein Grb2, and initiating branched actin assembly through the host nucleation promoting factor N-WASP.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: p14 binds the host cell adaptor protein Grb2.
source: Here we show that the reptilian orthoreovirus fusogen p14 accomplishes this by presenting a c-src kinase substrate in its cytoplasmic tail, binding the host cell adaptor protein Grb2, and initiating branched actin assembly through the host nucleation promoting factor N-WASP.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: p14 initiates branched actin assembly through the host nucleation promoting factor N-WASP.
source: Here we show that the reptilian orthoreovirus fusogen p14 accomplishes this by presenting a c-src kinase substrate in its cytoplasmic tail, binding the host cell adaptor protein Grb2, and initiating branched actin assembly through the host nucleation promoting factor N-WASP.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The p14 ectodomain cannot interact with apposing membrane through the ~2 nm repulsive hydration barrier.
source: Since p14 ectodomain extends only 0.7–1.5 nm from the plasma membrane (Corcoran et al., 2006), it cannot interact with apposing membrane through the ~2 nm repulsive hydration barrier.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known size of the p14 ectodomain and the hydration barrier, with citation support.

claim: The p14 ectodomain is able to disrupt and mix membranes when the hydration barrier is overcome by using divalent cations to bring bare membranes containing negatively charged PS together in vitro.
source: If that barrier can be overcome, for example by using divalent cations to bring bare membranes containing negatively charged PS together in vitro, the p14 ectodomain is able to disrupt and mix membranes (Top et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The primary role of branched actin network assembly by p14 is to physically push the fusogenic ectodomain into the opposing plasma membrane.
source: We propose that the primary role of branched actin network assembly by p14 is to physically push the fusogenic ectodomain into the opposing plasma membrane, a step normally carried out by conformational changes of tall fusogens.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Localized force generation by branched actin network assembly around p14's cytoplasmic domain drives close membrane apposition by coupling to and pushing against the cortical actin cytoskeleton.
source: In this model, localized force generation by branched actin network assembly around p14's cytoplasmic domain drives close membrane apposition by coupling to and pushing against the cortical actin cytoskeleton, much like other actin-based membrane protrusions.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The p14 ectodomain contains hydrophobic residues and myristoylation that are known to be necessary for fusion.
source: This close apposition in the presence of p14's membrane-disruptive ectodomain, which contains hydrophobic residues and myristoylation that are known to be necessary for fusion (Corcoran et al., 2004; Corcoran and Duncan, 2004; Top et al., 2009), may be sufficient to drive cell-cell fusion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton could promote clustering of p14 ectodomains into sub-diffraction-limited domains.
source: The actin cytoskeleton could promote clustering of p14 ectodomains into sub-diffraction-limited domains (Köster and Mayor, 2016), although enrichment of p14 or phosphorylated p14 was not readily observed at sites of fusion (Figure 5—figure supplement 2a,b,c and d).
evidence: This is speculation about a possible role of the actin cytoskeleton, with citation support and experimental observation.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton could change local membrane curvature and tension.
source: The actin cytoskeleton could also change local membrane curvature and tension (Kozlov and Chernomordik, 2015), block fusion pore closure, and/or actively expand the fusion pore (Kozlov and Chernomordik, 2015), all of which would promote cell-cell fusion by p14.
evidence: This is speculation about possible roles of the actin cytoskeleton, with citation support.

claim: Membrane fusion driven by other fusogens has long implicated the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Membrane fusion driven by other fusogens has long implicated the actin cytoskeleton (Kondo et al., 2015; Sanderson et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: Proposed roles of the actin cytoskeleton in fusion include regulating the activity, localization and enrichment of fusogens at fusion sites.
source: The proposed roles of the actin cytoskeleton include regulating the activity, localization and enrichment of fusogens at fusion sites (Yang et al., 2017), regulating protein-protein interactions (Wakimoto et al., 2013), and enlarging the fusion pore (Wurth et al., 2010; Zheng and Chang, 1990).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation support.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton has been suggested as a key player in cases where the putative fusogen remains unidentified or the mechanism of fusion remains unclear.
source: In cases where the putative fusogen remains unidentified or the mechanism of fusion remains unclear, the actin cytoskeleton has been suggested as a key player.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion.

claim: Examples of fusion processes where the actin cytoskeleton has been suggested as key include formation of signaling scaffolds and protrusive structures during osteoclast fusion.
source: Examples include formation of signaling scaffolds and protrusive structures during osteoclast fusion (Oikawa et al., 2012), macrophage fusion (Faust et al., 2019), and myoblast fusion in Drosophila (Kim et al., 2015; Sens et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Protrusive membrane structures generated by branched actin assembly have been observed at fusogenic synapses.
source: Protrusive membrane structures generated by branched actin assembly have also been observed at fusogenic synapses (Shilagardi et al., 2013) and can be formed in vitro (Liu et al., 2008a; Simon et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Myomixer is a short extracellular peptide that is required for myoblast fusion.
source: Our findings may be﻿ relevant to putative fusogens like myomixer, a short extracellular peptide that is required for myoblast fusion (Bi et al., 2018; Leikina et al., 2018; Millay et al., 2013; Quinn et al., 2017; Sampath et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2017) and does not resemble conformational-change based fusogens.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Myomixer does not resemble conformational-change based fusogens.
source: Our findings may be﻿ relevant to putative fusogens like myomixer, a short extracellular peptide that is required for myoblast fusion (Bi et al., 2018; Leikina et al., 2018; Millay et al., 2013; Quinn et al., 2017; Sampath et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2017) and does not resemble conformational-change based fusogens.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Myomixer, together with its partner myomaker, could harness the actin cytoskeleton to drive cell-cell fusion by physically forcing a short fusogenic ectodomain through dense cell surface proteins and into contact with an apposing membrane.
source: Like p14, myomixer, together with its partner myomaker, could harness the actin cytoskeleton to drive cell-cell fusion by physically forcing a short fusogenic ectodomain through dense cell surface proteins and into contact with an apposing membrane.
evidence: This is speculation about how myomixer might function, based on the findings with p14.

claim: Local forces generated by the cytoskeleton, rather than by conformational changes in a tall fusogen, provide a powerful tool for cells and pathogens to create multinucleated structures.
source: In this model of cell-cell fusion, local forces generated by the cytoskeleton, rather than by conformational changes in a tall fusogen, provide a powerful tool for cells and pathogens to create multinucleated structures.
evidence: This is a concluding statement summarizing the proposed model.
